source_refs.note: Discovery of sex linkage (PDF 105-106); Figure 18.14 is replaced by the original diagram. The book's F2 numbers add to 4255, not the printed 4252.

blocks.text: In 1910 Thomas Hunt Morgan found a male Drosophila with white eyes instead of the normal red. He crossed this mutant male with a normal (wild-type) red-eyed female, and all the F1 flies had red eyes, so red was dominant to white.

He then crossed red-eyed F1 flies with each other. The book reports 3473 red-eyed flies (males and females) and 782 white-eyed flies in the F2, about 18%. The ratio of red to white was greater than 3:1, but the striking point was that all the white-eyed F2 flies were males.

blocks.alt: Three crosses drawn with flies whose eyes are red or white. 1: red female XR XR x white male Xr Y gives red XR Xr daughters and red XR Y sons. 2: F1 x F1 gives XR XR, XR Xr, XR Y (red) and Xr Y (white), 3 red : 1 white with all whites male. 3: white female Xr Xr x red male XR Y gives red daughters and white sons. Below: a bar of 3473 red and 782 white F2 flies.
blocks.caption: Morgan's crosses with white-eyed Drosophila (original diagram after Figure 18.14).
blocks.long_description: Morgan crossed a white-eyed male with a red-eyed female and got an all red-eyed F1. In the F2 from F1 x F1 he found 3473 red-eyed flies of both sexes and 782 white-eyed flies, all male. A testcross of an F1 red female with a white male gave red and white females and males 1:1:1:1, proving white-eyed females can exist, and white females x red males gave red daughters and white sons. All of this fits if the eye-colour gene is on the X chromosome and the Y carries no allele for it: a male has a single X, so one recessive allele shows in him. Note: 3473 + 782 is 4255, while the book prints 4252; 782 is about 18% of either total.

blocks.text: To test whether a white-eyed female could exist, Morgan testcrossed an F1 red-eyed female with a white-eyed male and obtained white-eyed and red-eyed males and females in a 1:1:1:1 ratio, so females could have white eyes. He then mated a white-eyed female with a red-eyed male: all the daughters had red eyes and all the sons white eyes.

blocks.title: Morgan's conclusion
blocks.text: The white-eye gene is on the X chromosome, and the Y chromosome does not carry an allele of it. Morgan called such genes sex-linked genes and the traits sex-linked traits.

blocks.title: Checking the numbers
blocks.text: 3473 + 782 = 4255, while the book prints 4252 as the total; 782 is about 18% of either total.

blocks.prompt: Why did all of Morgan's white-eyed F2 flies turn out to be male?
blocks.explanation: The F1 female was XR Xr and the F1 male XR Y. Every daughter received the father's XR, so all were red-eyed; half the sons received the mother's Xr and, having no second X, were white-eyed.

items: Morgan 1910: white-eyed male x red female gave all-red F1.
F2: 3473 red, 782 white, all whites male.
White female x red male: red daughters, white sons; gene on X, none on Y.
